It is almost nine thousand meters high.
The air at the top is very thin and cold, so climbers carry oxygen.
Climbing Everest is one of the most difficult adventures.
In 2013, Raha Moharrak became the first Saudi woman to reach the top.
She showed that with hard work and courage, big dreams can come true.
The Amazon is the largest rainforest in the world.
It is in South America.
More than half of all the animal and plant types on Earth live in rainforests.
The poison dart frog is tiny, about the size of a paperclip, but it is one of the most dangerous animals in the rainforest.
Its bright colors, like blue, yellow and red, are a warning: 'Don't eat me!'
Interestingly, these frogs are not dangerous when they live in zoos, because their poison comes from the insects they eat in the wild.
Scientists are studying them to make new medicines.
A bee visits hundreds of flowers every day.
It collects nectar and takes it back to the hive.
The bees work together to make honey.
Ants live in big groups called colonies.
Each ant has a job.
The queen lays the eggs.
Worker ants find food, clean the nest and look after the babies.
Soldier ants protect the colony.
When an ant finds food, it leaves a special smell on the way back home, so other ants can follow the path.
That is why you often see ants walking in a line!

The Nile flows through eleven countries in Africa.
For thousands of years, farmers in Egypt depended on its water.
Every year, the river flooded and made the land rich for farming.
In Saudi Arabia, there are no permanent rivers, but there are many wadis.
Most of the year, a wadi is dry and sandy.
But after heavy rain, water rushes through it very fast, like a river.
These sudden floods can be dangerous, so people should never drive or camp in a wadi when rain is expected.
After the rain, wadis often turn green with grass and flowers for a few weeks.
There are only about five thousand wild tigers left in the world.
A hundred years ago, there were around one hundred thousand.
Many countries are now working hard to protect them.
Sea turtles have lived on Earth for more than one hundred million years, but today many of them are in danger.
They often eat plastic bags because they look like jellyfish.
Also, bright lights on beaches confuse baby turtles, so they walk away from the sea.
Volunteers now clean beaches, turn off lights at night and help the babies reach the water safely.
In the final match, our team was losing one-zero at half time.

You mustn't run near the pool.
You mustn't swim without a lifeguard.

Rule two: You mustn't give up, even if you are losing.

Children should be active for at least sixty minutes every day.
You can run, swim, ride a bike or play with friends.
Exercise makes your heart and muscles strong.
Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist.
It beats around one hundred thousand times a day, pumping blood to every part of your body.
When you exercise, your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster and you breathe more quickly.
Regular exercise makes your heart stronger, so it can pump more blood with fewer beats.
That's why athletes often have a slow heartbeat when they rest.
The first modern Olympic Games were in Athens in 1896.
Only a few countries took part.
Today, more than two hundred countries send athletes to the Olympics.
At the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney, Hadi Souan won a silver medal in the four hundred meters hurdles.
He became the first Saudi athlete to win an Olympic medal in running.
Years later, in 2012, Saudi women competed at the Olympics for the first time.
Every Olympics brings new stories of athletes who trained for years, failed many times and never stopped trying.
Ziad lost the chess final.
At first, he wanted to cry.
Then he shook hands with the winner and said 'Well done.'
His teacher said she was proud of him.
Thomas Edison, the famous inventor, once said that he had not failed; he had just found many ways that didn't work.
Many champions think the same.
Michael Jordan, one of the best basketball players ever, was not chosen for his school team when he was young.
He went home and cried, but then he practiced every day.
Losing can teach us more than winning, if we learn from it.
The Arabian horse is one of the oldest horse breeds in the world.
It has a small head, big eyes and a high tail.
Arabian horses are strong and very loyal to their owners.
Riding a horse is not just sitting on its back.
A good rider must understand the horse.
Horses can feel when a rider is nervous, so you must stay calm.
Before riding, you should brush the horse and check its hooves.
While riding, you control the horse with the reins and your legs, not by shouting.
After the ride, you must give the horse water and let it rest.
Respect is the secret of a great rider.
Here is the weather forecast for tomorrow.
In the north, it will be cold and windy.
In the east, it will be foggy in the morning.
In the south, there will be rain in the mountains.
In some winters, it snows in the north of Saudi Arabia, especially in the mountains near Tabuk.
When this happens, many families drive for hours to see it.
Children build snowmen and throw snowballs.
For people who live in a hot country, snow is a magical thing.
Weather scientists use satellites and computers to predict when the snow will come, so people can plan their trips.
Emperor penguins live in Antarctica.
In winter, the father penguin keeps the egg warm on his feet for about two months.
During this time, he doesn't eat anything!
The polar bear is the largest meat-eating animal on land.
Its fur looks white, but it is actually clear, and its skin underneath is black!
The black skin absorbs heat from the sun.
Polar bears are amazing swimmers and can swim for many hours.
They hunt seals from the ice.
But as the Arctic gets warmer and the ice melts, it is harder for them to find food.

They wear many thin layers instead of one thick layer, because warm air gets trapped between the layers.
They cover their heads, because we lose a lot of heat from our heads.
And they choose waterproof boots, because wet feet get cold very quickly.
In the desert at night, Bedouins wear a heavy wool cloak called a farwa for the same reason.

Water is special because we can find it in three states.
As a solid, it is ice.
As a liquid, it is the water we drink.
As a gas, it is water vapor, which we cannot see.
When you heat ice, it melts.
When you heat water, it evaporates and becomes vapor.
When the vapor cools down high in the sky, it forms clouds, and then it falls again as rain.
This journey is called the water cycle.

Since then, programmers call any mistake in their code a bug, and fixing it is called debugging.

She tells him funny stories about his father as a child.

Many families discovered that technology can bring people together, even when they are far apart.
The wheel was invented about five thousand years ago.
At first, people used it to make pots.
Later, they put wheels on carts, and travel became much easier.
About one thousand years ago, the scientist Al-Jazari lived in what is now Turkey.
He wrote a famous book about machines and designed more than fifty amazing inventions.
One of them was an elephant clock: a tall clock with a mechanical elephant and moving figures that showed the time.
Some of his ideas, like the crankshaft, are still used in engines today.
He is often called the father of robotics.

The Red Sea has some of the most beautiful coral reefs in the world.
Scientists have discovered that its corals can survive in warmer water than most other corals.
This makes them very special.
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, but about a quarter of all sea creatures depend on them.
Reefs are like underwater cities, full of fish, turtles, octopuses and sea stars.
But reefs are in danger.
When the ocean becomes too warm, corals lose the tiny plants that live inside them and give them color.
They turn white, and this is called coral bleaching.
If the water cools down quickly, the coral can recover.
If it doesn't, the coral may die.
Before you dive, you should always check your equipment.
Make sure your tank is full and your mask fits well.
Go down slowly, and never hold your breath with a tank.
Before oil was discovered, pearl diving was one of the most important jobs in the Gulf.
Divers went to sea for four months in the hot summer.
They had no tanks or masks.
A diver held his breath for one or two minutes, went down to the seabed with a stone tied to his foot, and collected oysters.
A rope connected him to a man on the boat, who pulled him up.
The work was very hard and dangerous, but the pearls of the Gulf were famous around the world.
A mother turtle comes to the beach at night.
She digs a hole and lays about one hundred eggs.
After about two months, the baby turtles hatch and walk to the sea.
Only about one in a thousand baby sea turtles survives to become an adult.
The journey is dangerous from the very first minute.
Crabs and birds wait on the beach, and fish wait in the water.
But the turtles that survive can live for more than fifty years.
Amazingly, many female turtles return to lay their eggs on the same beach where they hatched, even after swimming thousands of kilometers.
Scientists believe they use the Earth's magnetic field like a map.
Every year, about eleven million tons of plastic go into the ocean.
Some scientists say that by 2050, there could be more plastic than fish in the sea, if we don't change our habits.
In 2013, a young Dutch student named Boyan Slat had an idea.
He wanted to use the ocean's own currents to collect floating plastic.
Many experts said it wouldn't work.
But Boyan didn't give up.
He started a project called The Ocean Cleanup.
His team built long floating barriers that catch plastic while letting fish swim underneath.
Since then, they have removed huge amounts of plastic from the ocean and from rivers.
His story shows that one young person's idea can make a real difference.
In Bahrain, the old pearling path is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Visitors can walk past the old houses of pearl merchants and learn about the hard life of the divers.
When a diver came back to the boat with a basket of oysters, the crew opened them one by one.
Most were empty.
Sometimes there was a small, plain pearl.
Very rarely, a large, perfectly round, shining pearl appeared, and the whole crew celebrated.
The captain, called the nokhada, sold the pearls to merchants, who sent them to India and later to Europe.
Even though the divers worked hardest, they often earned the least money.
Their songs, called fijiri, are still sung today to remember their courage.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was built about four thousand five hundred years ago.
It was the tallest building in the world for almost four thousand years.
Thousands of workers built it.
For hundreds of years, nobody could read hieroglyphs.
Then, in 1799, soldiers found a stone near the town of Rosetta in Egypt.
The Rosetta Stone had the same text written in three scripts: hieroglyphs, another Egyptian script and ancient Greek.
Because scholars could read Greek, they could compare the texts.
In 1822, a French scholar named Champollion finally understood the hieroglyphs.
Suddenly, the walls of temples and tombs could tell their stories again.
Ibn Sina was born more than a thousand years ago.
He was a doctor and a writer.
His book, The Canon of Medicine, was used in universities in Europe for hundreds of years.
About twelve hundred years ago, Baghdad was one of the greatest cities of learning in the world.
Scholars came from many lands to study and work at the House of Wisdom.
They translated books from Greek, Persian and Indian into Arabic, and then they added their own discoveries.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote about algebra; his name gave us the word 'algorithm,' which computers use today.
Other scholars studied the stars, built observatories and made more accurate maps.
Their work later helped European scientists during the Renaissance.
The Silk Road was not one road.
It was a network of many routes over land and sea.
It was used for more than one thousand five hundred years and connected East Asia with Europe and Africa.
Paper was invented in China.
For centuries, the Chinese kept the secret of how to make it.
In the eighth century, papermaking reached the city of Samarkand, along the Silk Road, and soon after that, Baghdad opened its first paper mill.
Paper was cheaper and lighter than the old writing materials, so books became easier to make.
Libraries grew, and knowledge spread faster.
Later, the technique traveled to Spain and the rest of Europe.
A simple invention changed how the whole world learned.
Al Masmak Fort is in the center of Riyadh.
It was built about one hundred and fifty years ago from mud and clay.
Today, it is a museum that tells the story of the founding of the Kingdom.

At dawn, they captured Al Masmak Fort.
This event was the beginning of a long journey to unite most of the Arabian Peninsula.
Thirty years later, in 1932, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was officially established.
Today, visitors to the fort can still see the spearhead stuck in the old wooden door, a reminder of that famous morning.
A compass has a small magnet inside.

Sailors used compasses to find their way across the sea, even when they couldn't see the stars.
Mariam al-Ijliya lived in the city of Aleppo more than one thousand years ago.
Her father was an astrolabe maker, and she learned the craft from him.
Her astrolabes were so accurate and beautifully made that the ruler of the city employed her at his court.

In 1990, an asteroid was named '7060 Al-'Ijliya' in her honor.

Children can join workshops to make pottery or write their names in ancient scripts.
A good museum doesn't only show us the past; it helps us understand who we are today.

Small steps, repeated many times, lead to big changes.
If someone feels faint, help them sit or lie down.

Give them some fresh air, and if they don't feel better, call for help.

Germs are so small that you can't see them without a microscope.
Some germs are harmful and make us sick, but many are helpful.
For example, some live in our stomachs and help us digest food.
In the 1840s, a doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis noticed something strange in his hospital in Vienna.
Many mothers became very sick after giving birth.
He realized that doctors were going from one patient to another without washing their hands.
He told all the doctors to wash their hands before touching patients, and the number of sick mothers dropped dramatically.
Sadly, many doctors laughed at him and didn't believe him.
Years later, scientists proved that germs cause disease, and Semmelweis was finally recognized as a hero.
Carbohydrates like bread, rice and potatoes give us energy.
Protein helps our muscles grow and repair.
We need a little fat too, from foods like nuts and olive oil.

Keeping your room dark, quiet and cool also helps.
A regular routine, going to bed and waking up at the same time every day, even on weekends, trains your body to sleep better.
It's normal to feel frustrated when something is difficult.
When this happens, take a short break, drink some water, and then try again.
You can also ask someone for help.

Old houses often make strange sounds at night.
When the air gets colder, wood shrinks a little and makes cracking noises.
Pipes can also knock when water moves through them.

At night, people saw a light moving in the windows.

Recycling one aluminum can saves enough energy to run a TV for about three hours.
Aluminum can be recycled again and again, forever, without losing its quality.
Reducing is actually the most important of the three Rs.
Recycling is good, but it still uses energy and water.
The best rubbish is the rubbish we never make.
You can reduce waste by carrying a water bottle instead of buying plastic ones, choosing products with less packaging and buying only what you need.
Reusing comes second: old clothes can become cleaning cloths, and glass jars can store food.
Recycling is the last step, for things we cannot reduce or reuse.
Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity.
Saudi Arabia is building some of the biggest solar power plants in the world.
In the future, much more of the country's electricity will come from the sun.
Most of the world's electricity still comes from burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal.
These fuels formed from plants and animals that lived millions of years ago.
When we burn them, they release carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and makes the Earth warmer.
Renewable energy, such as solar and wind, produces electricity without burning anything.
The challenge is that the sun doesn't shine at night and the wind doesn't always blow, so scientists are developing better batteries to store the energy.
The Earth's average temperature has risen by more than one degree since the 1800s.
That might not sound like much, but it causes more heatwaves, stronger storms and melting ice.
The greenhouse effect is natural and actually important.
Gases in the atmosphere act like a blanket around the Earth, keeping it warm enough for life.
Without them, the Earth would be frozen.
The problem is that humans have added too many of these gases, making the blanket thicker.
More heat gets trapped, and the planet slowly warms.
Scientists around the world agree that we need to reduce these gases.
Countries are setting targets, and many cities are planting millions of trees, which absorb carbon dioxide.
Saudi Arabia has started a big project to plant ten billion trees in the coming decades.
The trees will help fight desertification, reduce dust storms and make cities cooler.
Wangari Maathai grew up in Kenya, where she saw forests being cut down and rivers drying up.
Women had to walk further and further to find firewood and water.
In 1977, she started the Green Belt Movement and encouraged women to plant trees.
At first, people laughed at the idea.
But the women kept planting, one seedling at a time.
Over the years, they planted more than fifty million trees.
In 2004, Wangari Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

A five-minute shower uses about forty liters of water.
A full bath can use more than one hundred liters.
Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth can save around twelve liters each time.
Most of the fresh water in the world is not used in homes, but on farms.
In hot, dry countries, a lot of water evaporates before it reaches the plants.
That's why drip irrigation is so useful.
Thin pipes with tiny holes deliver water drop by drop, directly to the roots.
This can save up to half of the water used in traditional methods.
Some farmers also water their plants in the early morning or evening, when it is cooler and less water evaporates.
When Ryan Hreljac was six years old, he learned that many children in Africa didn't have clean water.
He did extra chores to earn money and built his first well in Uganda.
His foundation has since helped build over a thousand water projects.
In 2013, two sisters from Bali, Melati and Isabel Wijsen, were twelve and ten years old.
They were tired of seeing plastic bags all over their beautiful island.
After a lesson about inspiring people, they decided to act.
They started a campaign called 'Bye Bye Plastic Bags.'
They organized beach clean-ups, collected thousands of signatures and spoke to the government.
Some people didn't take them seriously because they were children.
But the sisters were determined.
By 2019, Bali had officially banned single-use plastic bags.
Their campaign has since inspired young people in many countries.
Chocolate is made from cacao beans.
The beans are picked, dried and roasted.
Then they are ground into a paste, and sugar and milk are added.
Finally, the chocolate is poured into molds and cooled.
Have you ever wondered how a pencil is made?
First, graphite is mixed with clay and water.
The more clay is added, the harder and lighter the pencil will be.
The mixture is shaped into thin rods and baked in an oven.
Meanwhile, blocks of cedar wood are cut into thin slats, and grooves are cut into them.
The graphite rods are placed in the grooves, and a second slat is glued on top, like a sandwich.
The 'sandwich' is then cut into individual pencils, which are painted and stamped.
Billions of pencils are produced every year.
If I had a time machine, I would travel back one thousand years to visit the House of Wisdom in Baghdad.
I would talk to the scholars and ask them about their discoveries.
Our teacher asked us: 'If you could solve one problem in the world, what would it be?'
Faisal said he would end hunger, so no child would go to bed hungry.
Nora said she would invent a cheap way to clean the air in big cities.
Majid said he would build schools in villages that don't have any.
Then the teacher asked a harder question: 'What small step could you take now?'
Faisal decided to collect food for a local charity.
Nora started a plant-a-tree club.
Majid began sending books to a village school.
Big dreams, our teacher said, start with small actions.
In the ninth century, Abbas ibn Firnas, who lived in Cordoba, built a pair of wings from wood and feathers.
He jumped from a hill and glided for a short time before landing badly.
He is remembered as one of the first people who tried to fly.
In 1903, two brothers who owned a bicycle shop in the United States made history.
Orville and Wilbur Wright had studied birds for years to understand how they controlled their flight.
They built gliders and tested them hundreds of times.
Many attempts ended in crashes.
Finally, on December 17, 1903, their airplane, the Flyer, stayed in the air for twelve seconds and flew thirty-seven meters.
It was the first controlled, powered flight in history.
Today, millions of people fly every day, and it all started with two curious brothers who refused to give up.
Good designers start by asking questions.
Who will use this product?
What problem does it solve?
Then they draw ideas, build a simple prototype and ask real people to test it.
A group of students in Jeddah noticed that their grandparents often forgot to take their medicine.
They decided to design a solution.
First, they interviewed ten elderly people to understand the problem.
They learned that many of them didn't like using phones.
So instead of an app, the students designed a simple box with seven compartments, one for each day.
A light turns on at the right time, and the box makes a gentle sound.
After testing it with their grandparents, they made the buttons bigger because some users had weak eyesight.
Their project won first prize at the regional science fair.
In 1945, an engineer named Percy Spencer was working near a radar machine when he noticed that the chocolate bar in his pocket had melted.
This led to the invention of the microwave oven.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming, a Scottish scientist, went on holiday and left some dishes of bacteria on his desk.
When he came back, he noticed that a blue-green mold had grown on one of the dishes.
Around the mold, the bacteria had died.
Many people would have thrown the dish away, but Fleming was curious.
He discovered that the mold produced a substance that killed bacteria.
He called it penicillin.
Years later, other scientists found a way to produce it in large quantities, and penicillin became the first antibiotic.
It has saved millions of lives.
In a smart home, the curtains open automatically when the sun rises.
The air conditioner turns on before you arrive home.
And if someone rings the doorbell, you can see who it is on your phone, even if you are not at home.
Smart technology can be especially helpful for people who are elderly or have disabilities.
For example, a person who cannot walk easily can turn on lights, lock doors and adjust the temperature using only their voice.
Sensors can detect if an elderly person has fallen and automatically send a message to their family.
However, experts warn that smart devices collect a lot of personal information.
It is important to choose devices from trusted companies, use strong passwords and think carefully about what information we share.
Asia is the largest continent, and it has the biggest population.
Antarctica is the coldest continent, and nobody lives there permanently, except scientists who stay for a few months.
The Arabian Peninsula is the largest peninsula in the world.
A peninsula is land that is surrounded by water on three sides.
To the west is the Red Sea, to the east is the Arabian Gulf, and to the south is the Arabian Sea.
For thousands of years, its location, which connects Asia, Africa and Europe, made it an important center for trade.
Spices, incense and textiles that came from India and Africa passed through its ports and deserts on their way to the Mediterranean.
Ibn Battuta left his home in Tangier in 1325, when he was twenty-one years old.
He planned to be away for about two years, but he traveled for nearly thirty years.
Ibn Battuta is often called one of the greatest travelers in history.
Over three decades, he visited regions that are now more than forty countries, from West Africa to China.
He traveled by camel, by horse, on foot and by ship.
He survived storms, robbers and illness.
In many places he worked as a judge, because he had studied Islamic law.
When he finally returned home, the Sultan of Morocco asked a scholar named Ibn Juzayy to write down his stories.
The book, known as the Rihla, which means 'The Journey,' is still read today.
In many Arab countries, guests are served coffee with the right hand.
When a guest has had enough, they gently shake the small cup from side to side.
This tells the host 'Thank you, no more.'
A gesture that is polite in one country can be rude in another.
In many Western countries, people look directly into each other's eyes to show honesty, while in some East Asian cultures, looking down shows respect for older people.
In some countries, showing the bottom of your shoe is rude.
In Japan, it is polite to slurp your noodles, which shows you are enjoying the food, but this would seem rude in many other places.
Travelers who learn these customs before visiting usually find that people are warmer and more welcoming.
Arabic is spoken by more than four hundred million people and is one of the six official languages of the United Nations.
It is written from right to left and has twenty-eight letters.
Many English words actually came from Arabic.
When scholars in Europe translated Arabic books on science and mathematics in the Middle Ages, they borrowed many words.
'Algebra' comes from 'al-jabr.'
'Coffee' comes from 'qahwa.'
'Sugar' comes from 'sukkar,' and 'cotton' from 'qutn.'
Even 'zero' traveled from the Arabic 'sifr.'
Languages are like rivers that mix as they flow.
When you learn a new language, you often discover that it is more connected to your own than you thought.
Hegra, in AlUla, was Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It has more than one hundred tombs that were carved into sandstone by the Nabataeans about two thousand years ago.
The Taj Mahal in India is one of the most famous buildings in the world.
It was built in the seventeenth century by the emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
About twenty thousand workers built it over more than twenty years.
It is made of white marble, which changes color during the day: pink in the morning, white at noon and golden in the moonlight.
The building is perfectly symmetrical, and its gardens are divided into four parts, which represent the gardens of paradise.
Attention, please.
Flight SV 412 to Cairo has been delayed by two hours because of bad weather.
Passengers are asked to wait in the lounge.
Free drinks are offered at the café.
Dear Customer Service, I am writing to complain about my recent trip.
My flight from Riyadh to Kuala Lumpur, which was supposed to leave at 9 a.
m.
, was delayed for six hours.
Nobody explained the reason, and we were not offered any food.
When I arrived, I discovered that one of my bags had been lost.
I have attached the reference number that was given to me at the airport.
I would like my bag to be returned as soon as possible, and I would appreciate compensation for the delay.
Yours faithfully, Hind Al-Harbi.
Yesterday, the coach told the team that they had played very well.
He said that he was proud of them.
He also explained that they needed to practice passing before the next match.
Last week, our class interviewed the school nurse for the school newspaper.
Sara asked her how long she had worked at the school.
She said she had worked there for eight years.
Faisal asked what the most common problem was.
She told us that most students who came to her had headaches because they didn't drink enough water.
She explained that we should drink at least six glasses a day.
At the end, she said she hoped our article would help students stay healthy.
We promised that we would put her advice on the front page.
Here are today's headlines.
Local school wins national robotics competition.
New metro line opens in Riyadh.
Scientists discover new species of lizard in the Empty Quarter.
A news article usually answers six important questions, often called the five Ws and one H: Who?
What?
Where?
When?
Why?
and How?
The most important information comes in the first paragraph, which is called the lead.
Details come later.
This structure is called the 'inverted pyramid,' because the biggest and most important part is at the top.
Journalists use it because many readers only read the beginning of an article.
A good article is also fair: it presents different points of view and separates facts from opinions.
In the interview, the astronaut said that the hardest part of being in space was sleeping, because there is no up or down.
She said that the view of Earth was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen.
A good interviewer prepares carefully.
Before the interview, they research the guest's life and work.
They write open questions, which start with words like 'how,' 'why' or 'what,' because these encourage long, interesting answers.
Closed questions, which can be answered with 'yes' or 'no,' give less information.
During the interview, a good interviewer listens carefully and asks follow-up questions.
For example, if the guest says, 'That was the hardest year of my life,' the interviewer might ask, 'Why was it so hard?'
Listening is just as important as asking.
Fact: Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level.
Opinion: Hot chocolate is the most delicious drink in winter.
Facts can be checked; opinions show how someone feels.
Every day, false stories spread online, sometimes faster than true ones.
A fake photo of a shark swimming on a flooded highway has appeared after almost every big storm for years.
To avoid being tricked, ask yourself a few questions.
Who wrote this?
Is it from a trusted news source?
Does the headline seem designed to make me angry or scared?
Can I find the same story on other reliable websites?
You can also do a reverse image search to see where a photo first appeared.
Thinking before sharing is one of the most important skills in the digital age.
Good evening.
Tomorrow will be hot across most of the Kingdom, with temperatures reaching forty-six degrees in the east.
Dust storms are expected in the north, reducing visibility.
The Asir mountains will be cooler, with a chance of rain in the afternoon.
Weather forecasting has changed enormously.
Long ago, people predicted the weather by watching the sky, the wind and animals.
Today, meteorologists use satellites that orbit the Earth, radars that detect rain, and thousands of weather stations that measure temperature, pressure and humidity.
All this data is fed into supercomputers, which run complex models to predict how the atmosphere will change.
A five-day forecast today is as accurate as a one-day forecast was forty years ago.
Still, weather is chaotic, so forecasts always include some uncertainty.
In tennis news, the young champion won her third tournament this year.
She defeated the world number two in straight sets.
She told reporters that she was dedicating the win to her coach.
Sports reporting is not only about scores.
The best sports stories are about people.
When reporters write about a match, they describe the key moments, but they also explain what the result means for the team, the players and the fans.
They interview players after the game to understand how they felt.
Many famous sports stories are about comebacks: teams that were losing badly but never gave up.
Readers love these stories because they teach lessons that go far beyond sport, such as determination, teamwork and respect.
Yara gets fifty riyals a month.
She puts ten riyals in her charity box, saves twenty riyals and spends twenty on things she needs.
She calls this her 'three jars' plan.
When Hamad got two hundred riyals for Eid, his first idea was to spend it all on a new video game.
But his father suggested something different.
'What if you divided it?'
he asked.
'Spend some now, save some for something bigger, and give some to people who need it.'
Hamad thought about it.
He spent eighty riyals on a book and a ball, saved one hundred riyals toward a tablet he wanted, and gave twenty riyals to a charity for orphans.
Months later, when he finally bought the tablet, he said it felt much better than anything he had bought quickly.
Before you buy something, ask yourself three questions: Do I really need it?
Can I afford it?
Will I still want it next week?
If the answer to any question is no, wait.
Shops and advertisers use clever tricks to make us buy more.
Sweets are often placed near the cash register, where children wait with their parents.
Prices like 9.
99 look much cheaper than 10, even though the difference is tiny.
'Limited time offer' messages make us feel we must buy immediately.
Online, apps show us products that are similar to things we have already looked at.
Knowing these tricks helps us become smarter shoppers who make decisions with our heads, not just our feelings.
Last Saturday, Jana and her brother sold lemonade in front of their house.
They spent thirty riyals on supplies and sold forty cups for two riyals each.
They made a profit of fifty riyals.
When Ziyad started his small business selling homemade cookies at school events, his first day was a disaster.
He made one hundred cookies but sold only twenty, because he set the price too high and his table was in a corner where nobody walked.
Instead of giving up, he asked his customers for feedback.
They said the cookies were delicious but too expensive.
The next time, he lowered the price, moved to the entrance and offered free tastes.
He sold everything in an hour.
Ziyad learned that mistakes are lessons, if you are willing to listen and change.
When you deposit money in a bank, the bank keeps it safe.
Banks use this money to give loans to other people and businesses.
This helps people buy homes and start companies.
Thousands of years ago, there was no money.
People traded goods directly: a farmer might exchange wheat for a pair of shoes.
This is called barter.
The problem was that the shoemaker might not want wheat!
So people started using items that everyone valued, like salt, shells and later gold and silver coins.
Paper money came much later, first in China.
Today, much of our money is digital.
We pay with cards and phones, and the money moves between bank accounts as numbers on computers.
But the idea is the same: money is a tool that makes trading easier.
This new juice is made from one hundred percent fresh oranges.
There is no added sugar.
Buy two bottles and get the third one free!
Offer ends Sunday.
Advertisers carefully choose their target audience.
An advert for toys appears during children's programs, while an advert for cars appears during the evening news.
Many adverts use famous people, because we tend to trust people we admire.
Others use music and bright colors to create positive feelings.
Some adverts even show a product being used by happy families, suggesting that buying it will make us happy too.
Understanding these techniques doesn't mean we should never buy anything.
It means we can make our own decisions instead of letting adverts decide for us.
Every Ramadan, Rayan's school organizes a food basket campaign.
Students bring rice, oil, dates and sugar.
Last year, they prepared two hundred baskets for families in need.
Scientists have discovered something interesting: giving makes people happier.
In one study, people were given some money.
Half were told to spend it on themselves, and half were told to spend it on someone else.
At the end of the day, those who spent money on others reported feeling happier.
Other studies show that people who volunteer regularly often feel less stressed and more satisfied with life.
This matches a lesson that many cultures and religions have taught for centuries: the hand that gives is better than the hand that takes.
Scientists say that we remember things better when we review them several times with breaks in between.
This is called spaced repetition.
Studying for ten minutes every day is better than studying for one hour once a week.
For a long time, people believed that intelligence was fixed: you were either smart or not.
But scientists now know that the brain is like a muscle.
When you learn something new and practice it, connections between brain cells become stronger.
A psychologist named Carol Dweck called this idea a 'growth mindset.'
Students with a growth mindset believe they can get better with effort.
When they face a hard problem, they say 'I can't do this yet,' instead of 'I can't do this.'
Research shows that this small change in thinking can make a big difference in how much students learn.
Our class had a problem: the classroom was too noisy during group work.
We suggested three solutions: using quiet signals, making smaller groups, and working in the library.
We tried quiet signals first, and it worked!
Engineers use a process called design thinking to solve problems.
First, they empathize: they try to understand the people who have the problem.
Second, they define the problem clearly.
Third, they brainstorm many ideas without judging them.
Fourth, they build a simple prototype of the best idea.
Finally, they test it and use the results to improve it.
Then the cycle often starts again.
Design thinking has been used to create everything from better hospital beds to apps for farmers.
The secret is to focus on people and not to be afraid of trying, failing and trying again.
In today's debate, one team argued that school uniforms are good because they make everyone equal.
The other team argued that students should be able to express themselves through their clothes.
In the end, the judges said both teams had strong arguments.
Should children have their own mobile phones?
This is a popular debate topic.
Those who agree say that phones keep children safe, because parents can contact them at any time.
They add that phones can be useful for learning and that children need to learn how to use technology responsibly.
Those who disagree argue that phones can be distracting, can reduce sleep and can expose children to online dangers.
They suggest that children could use a simple phone without internet until they are older.
Most experts say the answer depends on the child's age, maturity and the rules the family sets.
Geese fly in a V shape.
The bird at the front works the hardest.
When it gets tired, it moves to the back, and another goose takes its place.
By working together, geese can fly much farther than one goose alone.
In 2018, twelve boys from a football team and their coach were trapped in a flooded cave in Thailand.
The rescue was one of the most difficult in history.
More than ten thousand people helped: divers from many countries, engineers, doctors, soldiers and volunteers who cooked food for the rescuers.
Some pumped water out of the cave; others searched for openings in the mountain.
After eighteen days, all thirteen were brought out safely.
The rescue showed the world what people can achieve when they work together for a common goal.
To remember the order of the planets, you can use this sentence: My Very Excellent Mother Just Served Us Nachos.
Each word starts with the same letter as a planet: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Memory champions can remember the order of a whole deck of fifty-two cards in less than a minute.
How do they do it?
Most of them use a technique called the 'memory palace,' which has been used since ancient Greece.
They imagine walking through a place they know well, like their home.
They place each piece of information at a specific spot, and they make the images funny or strange so they are easier to remember.
To recall the information, they simply 'walk' through the palace again in their mind.
The technique works because our brains are very good at remembering places and pictures.
During a brainstorm, there are no bad ideas.
Write down everything, even ideas that seem silly.
Sometimes a silly idea leads to a brilliant one.
Only after the brainstorm should you choose the best ideas.
George de Mestral, a Swiss engineer, went for a walk with his dog in 1941.
When they came home, both his trousers and the dog's fur were covered in small, sticky seeds called burrs.
Most people would have just pulled them off, but de Mestral was curious.
He looked at a burr under a microscope and saw hundreds of tiny hooks that caught onto loops in fabric and fur.
He spent years copying this design, and the result was Velcro.
This kind of creativity, which takes ideas from nature, is called biomimicry.
Today, engineers copy nature to design everything from fast trains to cool buildings.
Hessa wanted to know whether plants grow faster with music.
She took two identical plants, gave them the same water and light, but played music to only one of them.
After three weeks, she measured both plants and recorded the results.
Ibn al-Haytham, who lived in Cairo about a thousand years ago, is considered one of the first scientists to insist on experiments.
At the time, many thinkers believed that our eyes sent out rays to see objects.
Ibn al-Haytham doubted this.
He designed careful experiments with light, mirrors and a dark room with a tiny hole, and he showed that we see because light enters our eyes.
More importantly, he argued that a scientist should not trust any idea, even those of famous authorities, until it had been tested.
This principle is at the heart of the scientific method we use today.
The Earth's crust is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates.
These plates move a few centimeters every year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
When they push against each other, they can create mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes.
In the year 1256, a volcano erupted near Madinah.
Historical records describe how lava flowed for weeks and came close to the city, while fire could be seen from far away at night.
Fortunately, the lava stopped before reaching the city.
Today, scientists study Harrat Rahat, the volcanic field where the eruption happened, to understand the risks for the future.
Western Saudi Arabia lies near the Red Sea, where the African and Arabian plates are slowly moving apart.
This movement is gradually making the Red Sea wider, by about one centimeter each year.
Light travels at about three hundred thousand kilometers per second.
Sound is much slower: it travels at about three hundred and forty meters per second in air.
If you count the seconds between lightning and thunder and divide by three, you can estimate how many kilometers away the storm is.
Why is the sky blue?
Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow, each with a different wavelength.
When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it hits tiny molecules of gas.
Blue light, which has a short wavelength, is scattered in all directions much more than red light, which has a longer wavelength.
So when we look up, we see blue light coming from every part of the sky.
At sunset, sunlight has to travel through much more atmosphere to reach us.
Most of the blue is scattered away, leaving the beautiful oranges and reds.
Your brain weighs about one and a half kilograms, but it uses about twenty percent of your body's energy.
Even when you are resting, it is busy controlling your breathing, heartbeat and temperature.
For a long time, scientists thought that the adult brain could not change.
Today we know that the brain is 'plastic,' which means it can reorganize itself throughout life.
When you learn a new skill, such as playing an instrument or speaking a new language, new connections form between neurons.
The more you practice, the stronger and faster these connections become.
This is why learning feels difficult at first and easier later.
Interestingly, studies of London taxi drivers, who had memorized thousands of streets, found that a part of the brain related to memory and navigation had grown larger.
Metals such as copper are good conductors because electricity can flow through them easily.
Rubber, plastic and wood are insulators.
That's why electricians wear rubber gloves and use tools with plastic handles.
In the 1880s, two inventors had a famous rivalry that was later called the 'War of the Currents.'
Thomas Edison promoted direct current, or DC, which flows in one direction.
Nikola Tesla, together with businessman George Westinghouse, promoted alternating current, or AC, which changes direction many times per second.
AC had a big advantage: it could be sent over long distances much more efficiently.
Eventually, AC won, and it is still used to deliver electricity to our homes.
However, DC has made a comeback: batteries, phones, laptops and solar panels all use direct current.
The human body is made of about thirty trillion cells.
There are more than two hundred types, such as blood cells, nerve cells and muscle cells.
Each type has a special shape for its special job.
If you could stretch out the DNA inside just one of your cells, it would be about two meters long.
Yet it fits inside a nucleus that is too small to see without a microscope, because it is tightly coiled.
DNA is like an instruction manual, written in a code of only four chemical letters: A, T, C and G.
The order of these letters determines everything from the color of your eyes to how tall you might grow.
In 2003, scientists completed the Human Genome Project, reading the entire human genetic code for the first time.
This has helped doctors understand and treat many diseases.
The International Space Station travels at about twenty-eight thousand kilometers per hour.
Because it goes around the Earth so quickly, astronauts see about sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets every day.
In May 2023, Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni became the first Saudi astronauts to travel to the International Space Station.
Barnawi, a biomedical researcher, became the first Saudi woman, and among the first Arab women, to go to space.
During their mission of about ten days, they carried out more than a dozen scientific experiments, including research on stem cells and on how the brain is affected by weightlessness.
They also spoke by video to thousands of Saudi students, who watched them release a small kite to show how objects behave in microgravity.
Their mission inspired a new generation to dream about careers in space science.
In 2021, the Hope Probe, sent by the United Arab Emirates, reached Mars.
It was the first interplanetary mission by an Arab country.
It studies the Martian atmosphere to understand how the planet lost most of its air and water.
Sending humans to Mars would be the greatest journey in history, but the challenges are enormous.
The trip would take about seven months each way.
On Mars, temperatures can drop below minus one hundred degrees Celsius, and there are huge dust storms that can cover the entire planet.
Because the atmosphere is thin, astronauts would be exposed to dangerous radiation.
Communication is also difficult: a message from Mars can take up to twenty minutes to reach Earth, so astronauts would have to solve emergencies on their own.
Scientists are working on solutions, such as producing oxygen from the Martian atmosphere, which a NASA experiment has already succeeded in doing on a small scale.
Many stars have Arabic names, because Arab astronomers studied and recorded them more than a thousand years ago.
For example, the star Aldebaran comes from 'al-dabaran,' which means 'the follower,' and Betelgeuse also comes from an Arabic name.
When you look at a star, you are looking into the past.
The light from the nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, takes more than four years to reach us.
Light from some distant galaxies has been traveling for billions of years, which means we see them as they were long before the Earth existed.
In 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope began sending back images of galaxies that formed not long after the universe began.
By studying this ancient light, astronomers hope to answer some of the biggest questions: How did the first stars form?
And are we alone in the universe?
The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched by the Soviet Union in 1957.
It was about the size of a beach ball and sent a simple beeping signal.
Today, there are thousands of active satellites orbiting the Earth.
In 1985, Prince Sultan bin Salman became the first Arab and the first Muslim to travel to space.
He flew on the American space shuttle Discovery as part of a mission that launched an Arab communications satellite, Arabsat.
During the seven-day mission, he took photographs of the Arabian Peninsula and conducted experiments.
He later described how seeing the Earth from space changed his perspective: from space, he said, borders disappear, and you see one planet that all humans share.
Decades later, Saudi Arabia established a national space agency to develop its space program further.
On July 20, 1969, the Apollo 11 lunar module landed on the Moon.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface for about two and a half hours, while Michael Collins stayed in orbit.
When Apollo 11 landed, the astronauts had only about twenty-five seconds of fuel left.
The computer had been showing alarms because it was overloaded, and the planned landing site was full of large rocks.
Armstrong took manual control and flew the lunar module over the boulders until he had found a safe, flat area.
Back in Mission Control, people had been holding their breath.
When Armstrong finally said, 'The Eagle has landed,' the room exploded with relief.
The success depended not only on brave astronauts but also on around four hundred thousand engineers, scientists and workers who had built the rockets and the software.
In the past, rockets were used only once and then lost in the ocean.
Today, some companies land their rockets back on Earth and use them again.
This has reduced the cost of launching satellites dramatically.
As space becomes more accessible, new questions arise.
Should companies be allowed to mine asteroids for valuable metals?
If humans build bases on the Moon, who will make the rules there?
An international agreement from 1967, the Outer Space Treaty, says that no country can claim the Moon or other celestial bodies as its own, and that space should be used for peaceful purposes.
However, the treaty was written long before private space companies existed.
Many experts believe the world needs new agreements to make sure that space remains a place of cooperation, not competition and conflict.
Every good story has a problem.
The main character wants something, but something stands in their way.
This is called the conflict.
Without conflict, a story would be boring because nothing interesting would happen.
The tales of Sindbad the Sailor, from the collection known as One Thousand and One Nights, follow a clear story structure.
In each voyage, Sindbad, a merchant from Baghdad, sets sail in search of adventure and wealth.
The setting changes from busy ports to mysterious islands.
Soon, a conflict appears: a shipwreck, a giant bird called the roc, or a monstrous creature.
The tension rises until the climax, when Sindbad must use his intelligence to escape.
In the resolution, he returns home richer and wiser, only to feel restless again and begin another voyage.
At the start of the new school year, our teacher played a game to break the ice.
Everyone had to say one surprising fact about themselves.
By the end of the lesson, we were laughing together like old friends.
Idioms are expressions whose meaning cannot be understood from the individual words.
If someone says 'It's raining cats and dogs,' they don't mean animals are falling from the sky; they mean it's raining heavily.
Every language has its own idioms, and they often reflect the culture.
In Arabic, we might say that someone's 'eye is cold' to mean they feel relieved and happy, because in a hot climate, coolness is pleasant.
In English, which developed in a cold climate, 'warm' is often used for positive feelings, as in 'a warm welcome.'
Learning idioms helps you understand not only a language but also the way its speakers see the world.
In ancient Arabia, the market of Ukaz was famous for its poetry competitions.
Poets came from all over the peninsula to recite their best poems.
The most admired poems were remembered and repeated for generations.
Al-Mutanabbi, who lived over a thousand years ago, is often considered one of the greatest poets in the Arabic language.
Many of his verses have become proverbs that people still quote today, often without knowing who wrote them.
He was famous for his confidence and for his powerful use of language.
Poetry works through sound as well as meaning: rhythm makes it musical, rhyme makes it memorable, and images like metaphors help us see familiar things in a new way.
That is why a single line of poetry can stay in our minds for a lifetime, while a long paragraph is quickly forgotten.
Kalila wa Dimna was originally written in Sanskrit in India.
It was translated into Persian and then, in the eighth century, into Arabic by Ibn al-Muqaffa.
From Arabic, it spread to many other languages around the world.
In one of the fables of Kalila wa Dimna, a group of doves was caught in a hunter's net.
Each dove tried to escape alone, flapping desperately, but the net only grew tighter.
Then their wise leader told them: 'If we work together, we can lift the net.'
On her signal, all the doves flew up at the same moment, carrying the net into the sky.
They flew to their friend, a mouse, who chewed through the ropes and set them free.
The moral is clear: unity gives strength, and true friends help each other in times of trouble.
Good writers use all five senses.
Don't just describe what a place looks like.
Describe how it sounds, smells, feels and even tastes.

Compare these two openings.
First: 'It was a scary night.
Ali was afraid.'
Second: 'The wind howled through the broken window.
Ali pulled the blanket over his head, but he could still hear it: slow footsteps, coming up the stairs.'
The second version is far more powerful.
It shows rather than tells, it uses sound to create atmosphere, and it ends with a question in the reader's mind: who is coming?
Professional writers rarely get their opening right the first time.
Many rewrite their first page dozens of times, because they know that the first few lines decide whether a reader will keep going.

Book Review: 'The Lost Map of the Empty Quarter.'
This exciting adventure novel follows two cousins, Lama and Saud, who discover an old map in their grandfather's house.
The map leads them deep into the desert, where they must rely on traditional knowledge, like reading the stars and finding water, to survive.
The author's descriptions of the desert are beautiful; you can almost feel the heat and see the endless dunes.
The cousins' relationship, which begins with constant arguments, slowly turns into deep trust.
My only criticism is that some chapters are a little predictable.
Overall, I highly recommend it for readers aged ten and above.
A good leader doesn't only give orders.
A good leader listens to the team, explains the goal clearly and helps every member use their strengths.
When the team succeeds, a good leader shares the credit.
There is an old saying: 'The leader of a people is their servant.'
It reflects an idea that modern business experts call 'servant leadership.'
In this approach, the leader's main job is to support the team, removing obstacles, providing resources and helping each person grow.
Research suggests that teams with servant leaders are often more creative and more loyal, because people feel valued.
This doesn't mean that the leader avoids making difficult decisions.
It means the leader makes decisions with the team's well-being in mind, and is willing to be held accountable for them.
Studies show that many people are more afraid of public speaking than of spiders or heights.
But the fear can be reduced.
Practicing in front of a mirror, recording yourself, and speaking to small groups first can all help build confidence.
Many great speeches are remembered for one powerful phrase.
In 1963, Martin Luther King Jr.
repeated 'I have a dream' to describe a future of equality, and the repetition made his message unforgettable.
Skilled speakers use techniques like this deliberately.
They use the 'rule of three,' grouping ideas in threes because the brain finds them easy to remember.
They tell personal stories, because stories create emotion.
And they use pauses, because a moment of silence before an important point makes the audience lean in.
A speech is not just information; it is a performance that aims to move people.

Experts say that successful negotiators focus on interests, not positions.
A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why they want it.
Imagine a student council negotiating with the principal about a longer break.
The students' position is 'thirty minutes instead of twenty.'
Their interest is having enough time to eat and play.
The principal's position is 'no change,' but his interest is not losing lesson time.

Once both sides understood each other's interests, they found a creative solution: the break stayed at twenty minutes, but students were allowed to eat their snacks during the first lesson's last five minutes.
Both sides were satisfied.
Every child has rights.
The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989, says that all children have the right to education, health care, play and protection from harm.
One of the oldest known written legal codes is the Code of Hammurabi, which was created in ancient Babylon almost four thousand years ago.
It was carved on a large stone so that everyone could see the laws.
Before written laws existed, rules could be changed by whoever was in power.
Writing them down was an important step toward fairness, because the same rules applied to everyone and could be checked.
Today, the idea that nobody is above the law, called the rule of law, is considered one of the foundations of a just society.
During Hajj season, thousands of young Saudi volunteers help pilgrims.

Volunteering is seen not only as a way to help others but also as a way to build skills.
A study of young volunteers found that they developed communication, leadership and problem-solving abilities, which later helped them at university and work.
However, experts say that the best volunteering is based on real community needs.
Before starting a project, it's important to ask people what they actually need, rather than assuming.
A small, well-planned project often has more impact than a large one that doesn't match the community's needs.

When the student council of a girls' school in Riyadh decided to organize a charity bazaar, they divided the work carefully.

Two days before the event, they discovered that they didn't have enough tables.
Because they had kept a small emergency budget, they could rent extra ones.
The bazaar raised more than twelve thousand riyals for a children's hospital.
AI is already part of our daily lives.
It recommends videos, translates languages, helps doctors read scans and filters spam from our email.
Most of the time, we don't even notice it.
An AI system is only as good as the data it learns from.
If an AI is trained mostly on photos of one group of people, it may perform badly when it sees others.
This problem is called bias.
For example, some early face-recognition systems made many more mistakes with darker skin tones, because they had been trained on unbalanced data.
Researchers are now working to build fairer systems by using more diverse data and by testing their tools carefully.
Many experts argue that humans must always remain responsible for important decisions, such as medical diagnoses or job applications, and that AI should support people, not replace their judgment.
Experts predict that many children in school today will work in jobs that don't exist yet.
Twenty years ago, jobs like app developer and drone pilot were almost unknown.
That's why learning how to learn is so important.
When automated teller machines, or ATMs, appeared in the 1970s, many people predicted that bank tellers would lose their jobs.
Surprisingly, the number of bank employees in many countries actually increased for decades.
Because ATMs made it cheaper to run a branch, banks opened more branches, and employees moved from counting cash to helping customers with more complex needs.
History shows that technology often changes jobs more than it destroys them.
However, this change can be difficult for workers whose skills become outdated.
That's why governments and companies increasingly support lifelong learning, so that people can keep developing new skills throughout their careers.

Designing cities for hot climates requires special thinking.
Traditional Arabian towns were built with narrow alleys, thick mud walls and inner courtyards, which created shade and natural ventilation long before air conditioning existed.
Wind towers, called barjeel, caught breezes and directed them into the house.
Today, architects are rediscovering these ideas.
Modern sustainable designs combine traditional techniques, such as shaded streets and courtyards, with new technology, like solar panels and smart sensors that control cooling.
The lesson is that the most innovative solutions sometimes come from looking carefully at the past.

Imagine a self-driving car that suddenly faces an unavoidable accident.
Should it protect its passengers at all costs, or try to minimize harm to everyone, including pedestrians?
Questions like this used to belong only to philosophy classes, but now engineers must program real answers into real machines.

A large online experiment called the Moral Machine collected millions of responses from people in over two hundred countries and territories, and it found that people's answers varied depending on their culture.
This shows that technology is never just technical: it reflects human values.
That is why many universities now teach ethics alongside computer science.
The Haramain High-Speed Railway connects Makkah and Madinah through Jeddah.
Its trains can travel at up to three hundred kilometers per hour, making the journey between the two holy cities much faster.
Transport is responsible for a large share of the world's greenhouse gas emissions, so changing how we move is essential for the planet.
Electric cars are part of the solution, but they are not enough on their own.
If every car were electric, cities would still suffer from traffic jams and would still need huge amounts of space for roads and parking.
Many urban planners argue that the real future lies in combining several solutions: efficient public transport, safe routes for walking and cycling, and shared vehicles.
Cities that have invested in these options, such as Copenhagen, where many people cycle to work, show that it is possible to have cleaner air and less traffic at the same time.

Describe your dreams, your fears and the person you hope to become.

Don't give up.
With love, your younger self.
