He has a big field and many palm trees.
He drives a red tractor.
Every autumn, he picks the dates with my uncles.
A farmer's day starts before the sun comes up.
First, Abu Fahad feeds the cows and the chickens.
Then he checks the water for his plants.
In the afternoon, it is too hot to work, so he rests in the shade.
In the evening, he works in the field again.
His tomatoes and cucumbers are sold at the market.
He says farming is hard, but he loves to see things grow.
Near our house, builders are making a new mosque.
They work from early morning.
A big crane lifts the heavy bricks.
All the builders wear yellow helmets.
Building a house takes many months and many people.
First, an engineer draws a plan.
Then the builders dig the ground and make strong foundations.
They use bricks, cement and steel.
Electricians put in the wires, and plumbers put in the pipes for water.
At the end, painters paint the walls.
When the family moves in, they thank everyone who helped.
The fire alarm rings at school.
The children walk out quickly and quietly.
They stand in lines in the playground.
The teacher counts everyone.
It is only a practice.
Firefighters have a very important job.
When there is a fire, they drive to it in a big red truck.
They use long hoses to spray water on the fire.
They also climb ladders to save people from tall buildings.
Firefighters wear special clothes that protect them from heat.
They visit schools to teach children about fire safety.
They say never play with matches and always know two ways out of a room.
Last Friday, my family visited a farm.
We fed the goats with carrots.
I rode a white horse.
Then we drank fresh camel milk.
Last weekend, our class went on a trip to a farm outside the city.
The bus ride took one hour.
The farmer showed us how to milk a goat.
It was harder than I thought!
We collected eggs from the chickens and put them in a basket.
Then we had a picnic under the palm trees.
On the way home, everyone was tired but happy.
On Saturday, I rode my bike in the park.
Suddenly, the tyre was flat.
I walked home with my bike.
My dad and I fixed it with his tools.
Last weekend, Rashid had a problem.
He wanted to ride to his friend's house, but his bike chain was broken.
He felt sad because he could not go.
His grandfather saw him and said they could fix it together.
They found a new chain in the shop near their house.
Grandpa showed Rashid how to put it on.
It took one hour, but the bike worked again.
Rashid learned something new.
On Friday, we visited Grandpa.
He made tea for my parents.
He showed me old photos.
In one photo, he was a young boy with a camel.
Every Friday, we have lunch at my grandfather's house.
Last Friday, all my cousins came too.
Grandpa told us a story about his first trip to Makkah many years ago.
He went by car, and the journey took three days.
There were no big roads then.
After lunch, we played in his garden and picked lemons from his tree.
Before we left, Grandpa gave each of us a big hug.
Last weekend, we went camping in the desert.
We put up a big tent.
At night, we sat around the fire.
The moon was full and very bright.
Camping in the desert is a family tradition for us.
Last weekend, we drove for two hours from the city.
My father chose a place between two big sand dunes.
We set up the tents and collected wood for the fire.
My mother cooked rice and meat in a big pot.
After dinner, my uncle pointed at the stars and told us their names.
I fell asleep looking at the sky.
On Sunday, Mona lost her library card.
She looked in her bag and under her bed.
Finally, she found it inside her book.
Last Saturday, Ziyad found a brown wallet in the mall.
Ziyad did not keep it.
He took it to the information desk with his mother.
The man at the desk called the owner.
An old man came quickly and thanked Ziyad many times.
He was very happy because his photos were inside the wallet.
Ziyad felt proud because he did the right thing.
Yesterday was Dad's birthday.
We made a big card for him.
My sister baked a cake.
When Dad came home, we all shouted surprise.
He laughed and hugged us.
Last week, our teacher, Miss Huda, was leaving our school.
The class wanted to say thank you in a special way.
We had a secret plan.
Every student wrote a letter about their favorite memory with her.
Reem drew a big picture of our class.
On her last day, we put the letters and the picture in a box.
When Miss Huda opened it, she cried happy tears.
She said she would never forget us.
Mum gives Salem a shopping list.
He needs to buy eggs, bread and tomatoes.
He takes a cloth bag and goes to the shop with his father.
Every Thursday, I help my mother with the weekly shopping.
Before we go, we check the fridge and the cupboards.
I write the list in my best handwriting.
At the supermarket, I push the trolley and find the things on the list.
My mother teaches me to compare prices.
Sometimes the big packet is cheaper.
When we get home, I put everything in its place.
Every evening, Huda waters the garden.
She gives water to the roses and the small lemon tree.
She does not water at noon because the sun is too hot.
Our house has a small garden with flowers, mint and a lemon tree.
My job is to water it.
In summer, I water it every day, but in winter, only two times a week.
I learned that too much water is bad for plants.
Their roots need air too.
I put my finger in the soil to check if it is dry.
Last month, our lemon tree gave us twenty lemons!
My toy car does not work.
Dad opens it with a small screwdriver.
He puts in a new battery.
Now my car runs across the floor again.
When something breaks in our house, we try to fix it before we throw it away.
Last week, the arm of my sister's doll came off.
We used strong glue to put it back.
We waited one night for the glue to dry.
My puzzle box was broken too, so I used tape.
Fixing things saves money and is good for the planet.
My grandmother says old things have stories.
My baby brother is six months old.
When he cries, I make funny faces.
He smiles and laughs.
Then Mum gives him his bottle and he sleeps.
Having a baby in the house changes everything.
My little sister, Lulu, was born in the summer.
At first, she slept most of the day and cried at night.
Now she is bigger and loves to play.
I help my mother by bringing clean clothes and her toys.
When Mum is busy, I read picture books to Lulu.
She cannot understand the words, but she likes to look at the colors.
On Saturday, Fatima and her father cook lunch together.
They make chicken and rice.
Fatima washes the rice.
Her father cuts the onions.
The food smells very good.
Cooking with your family is fun, and you learn a lot.
Last week, my brother and I made pancakes with my mother.
First, we read the recipe together.
We mixed flour, eggs and milk in a big bowl.
My mother cooked them in a hot pan because it is not safe for children.
We put honey and banana on top.
They were the best pancakes ever.
Next time, we want to try a new recipe.
On Thursday afternoon, the whole family cleans the house.
Dad washes the windows.
Mum mops the kitchen floor.
My brother and I tidy our room and fold our clothes.
In our house, everyone has a job.
We have a chart on the fridge with our names and our jobs.
This week, I take out the rubbish and water the plants.
My sister clears the table after dinner.
My little brother puts his toys back in the box.
When we finish our jobs, we get a star on the chart.
At the end of the month, the person with the most stars chooses the Friday trip.
Every morning before sunrise, the fishermen of the village take their small boats out to sea.
They throw their nets into the water and wait.
By noon they come back to the harbour and sell their fish at the market.
Before oil was discovered, many families in the Gulf lived from the sea.
Men went fishing and pearl diving for months at a time.
Their wooden boats, called dhows, were built by hand without any plans on paper.
Today, most fishermen use boats with engines and modern nets, but some old dhows still sail along the coast.
In many towns, you can still visit the fish market early in the morning and watch the fishermen sell their catch.
Dolphins live in groups called pods.
They talk to each other with clicks and whistles.
Dolphins are very smart, and they can learn many things.
They often swim next to boats and jump out of the water.
Dolphins are some of the cleverest animals in the sea.
Scientists have watched dolphins use tools, for example, putting a sea sponge on their nose to protect it while they look for food.
A mother dolphin stays with her baby for several years and teaches it how to hunt.
Dolphins sleep with one half of their brain at a time, so they can still come up for air.
In the waters of the Gulf, you can sometimes see dolphins from the beach.
The lighthouse stands on a small island near the harbour.
At night its bright light turns around and around.
Ships can see it from very far away, so they know where the rocks are.
Long ago, lighthouse keepers lived alone or with their families next to the light.
Every evening they climbed the stairs to light the lamp, and every few hours they cleaned the glass so the light would stay bright.
During storms, they stayed awake all night.
Today, most lighthouses work by themselves with electric lights and computers.
Some old lighthouses have become museums where visitors can learn about the brave keepers who saved many sailors.
Reem and her brother are walking along the beach.
The tide is out, so there is a lot of wet sand.
They are collecting shells in a red bucket.
Suddenly, a small crab runs sideways in front of them.
Every shell on the beach was once the home of a small sea animal.
When the animal grows, some of them, like the hermit crab, need to find a bigger shell to live in.
That is why you should check that a shell is empty before you take it.
Sand is also interesting.
Much of it is made of tiny pieces of rock and broken shells that the waves have rubbed for thousands of years.
So when you build a sandcastle, you are using very old material.
Khalid is learning to dive.
His teacher shows him how to breathe from the tank.
Under the water, everything is quiet.
Khalid sees a turtle swimming slowly past him.
Coral reefs are like underwater cities.
They look like rocks or plants, but corals are actually tiny animals that live together in huge groups.
About a quarter of all sea creatures live on or near coral reefs.
Fish use the reefs to hide from bigger hunters and to find food.
Unfortunately, coral reefs are in danger because the seas are getting warmer.
Divers and scientists are working hard to protect them.
The sailors were fishing when the sky suddenly became dark.
The wind was getting stronger and the waves were very high.
The captain called the harbour on the radio.
They sailed back carefully and arrived safely.
Storms at sea can be very dangerous, even for big ships.
Before a trip, a good captain always checks the weather report.
If a storm is coming, it is better to stay in the harbour.
All boats must carry life jackets for everyone on board.
When a boat is in trouble, the crew can send a message by radio, and rescue teams will come by boat or helicopter.
These teams train for many hours so they are ready when someone needs help.
The moon goes around the Earth in about one month.
It has no light of its own.
When we see the whole bright circle, we call it a full moon.
The moon is covered in rocks, dust and craters.
The moon is the only place outside the Earth where people have walked.
Twelve astronauts visited it between nineteen sixty-nine and nineteen seventy-two.
Because there is no wind or rain on the moon, their footprints are probably still there today.
The moon also helps us on Earth.
Its pull makes the tides of the sea go up and down.
In many cultures, including ours, the moon is used to count the months of the year.
There are eight planets in our solar system.
Mercury is the closest to the sun.
Jupiter is the biggest planet, and Saturn is famous for its rings.
Earth is the only planet with life that we know of.
The planets can be divided into two groups.
The four planets closest to the sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky.
The four outer planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, are giant balls of gas and ice.
Venus is the hottest planet, even hotter than Mercury, because its thick clouds trap the heat.
Neptune is so far away that one year there is equal to about one hundred and sixty-five years on Earth.
Astronauts on the space station have a busy day.
They wake up early and check their emails from Earth.
They spend most of the day doing experiments.
In the evening, they exercise and then talk to their families.
Living in space is very different from living on Earth.
Without gravity, water does not pour, so astronauts drink from bags with straws.
Their food is in packets, and they must be careful that crumbs do not float into the machines.
Their muscles and bones become weaker in space, so they must exercise for two hours every day.
Saudi astronauts have visited the space station too, and they did science experiments that could help people on Earth.
Last night, Faisal and his grandfather went to the desert to look at the stars.
There were no city lights, so the sky was full of stars.
Grandpa showed him how to find the North Star.
Then they saw a shooting star.
For thousands of years, people have used the stars to find their way.
Arab travellers in the desert and sailors at sea learned the positions of the stars by heart.
Many stars still have Arabic names today, such as Aldebaran and Altair, because Arab scientists studied them carefully a thousand years ago.
Stars look small, but many are much bigger than our sun.
They only look tiny because they are very, very far away.
The rocket is standing on the launch pad.
Everyone is counting down from ten.
At zero, the engines roar and fire comes out.
The rocket rises slowly at first and then faster and faster.
A rocket needs a huge amount of power to escape the Earth's gravity.
Most of a rocket is actually fuel.
As the fuel burns, hot gas shoots out of the bottom and pushes the rocket up.
Some modern rockets can land again after the launch, so they can be used many times.
This makes space travel cheaper.
Many countries, including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, now have their own space programmes.
The space station goes around the Earth every ninety minutes.
That means the astronauts see sixteen sunrises every day!
They work as a team from different countries.
They send photos and messages to students on Earth.
The International Space Station is the biggest object people have ever put into space.
It is about as long as a football field and has been home to astronauts since the year two thousand.
Fifteen countries worked together to build it, piece by piece.
Inside, there are laboratories, a kitchen, a gym and small bedrooms.
Life is not easy there, but the astronauts say that the view of the Earth makes everything worth it.
Sami and his sister had a race in the park.
Sami was faster at the start, but his sister had more energy.
In the end, she ran faster than him and won the race.
Animals move at very different speeds.
A cheetah can run at more than one hundred kilometres an hour, but only for a short time.
A camel is much slower, but it can walk for many hours without stopping.
A garden snail is one of the slowest animals; it would need about a week to travel one kilometre.
Faster is not always better.
Each animal has the speed that it needs to survive in its home.
Last summer, Mona visited the tallest building in the world.
The lift was very fast.
From the top, the cars looked like small toys.
The people looked smaller than ants.
For a long time, the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest building in the world.
It kept that record for almost four thousand years.
Today, the tallest building is the Burj Khalifa, which is more than eight hundred metres high.
A new tower in Jeddah is planned to be even taller.
Building very tall towers is difficult because of strong winds.
Engineers design special shapes that help the wind move around the building.
In the museum, Huda saw an old phone.
It was bigger and heavier than her mother's phone.
It had a round dial with numbers.
Her grandmother said she used one like that when she was young.
Fifty years ago, life in our cities was very different.
There were fewer cars and the roads were narrower.
Houses were built of mud and stone, and they had thick walls to keep them cool.
Today, our houses are bigger and have air conditioners, but many people still love the old style.
In Riyadh, the old Diriyah district has been rebuilt so that visitors can see how people lived in the past.
Ahmed wants new football boots.
The first pair costs ninety riyals, and the second pair costs one hundred and fifty.
The second pair is more expensive, but it is stronger.
Ahmed decides to save his money for the better pair.
When you go shopping, it is smart to compare before you buy.
First, look at the price, but don't stop there.
Think about how long the thing will last.
A cheap toy that breaks after one week can be more expensive in the end than a better toy that lasts for years.
It is also a good idea to read what other buyers say.
Finally, ask yourself an important question: do I really need it, or do I just want it?
Lina lives near her school, so she walks there every day.
Her cousin Nora lives far away in another city.
Nora's school is twenty kilometres from her house, so she goes by bus.
Distances in our country can be very large.
Driving from Riyadh to Jeddah takes about ten hours, but a plane takes less than two.
In the past, the same journey took weeks on camels.
Today, new fast trains connect some cities.
The train between Makkah and Madinah takes about two hours and travels at three hundred kilometres an hour.
Thanks to modern transport, far places feel much nearer than before.
Yesterday was the best day of the holiday.
In the morning, we went to the beach.
In the afternoon, we ate the most delicious fish.
The worst part was when it was time to go home.
Our teacher asked us to write about the best day of our lives.
Some students wrote about winning a prize or getting a present.
Sara wrote about a simple day.
She said that her best day was when the electricity went off at night, and the whole family sat together on the roof.
They told stories, looked at the stars and laughed for hours.
The teacher said that the best days are often the ones we spend with people we love.
Faisal lives on the ninth floor.
Every day he takes the lift down to the ground floor.
One day the lift was being repaired, so he had to walk down the stairs.
It took him five minutes.
Before the safe lift was invented, buildings were rarely taller than six floors because people did not want to climb so many stairs.
Early lifts were dangerous because the rope could break.
In eighteen fifty-three, Elisha Otis showed a lift with a special brake.
If the rope broke, the brake would stop the lift from falling.
His invention made tall buildings possible.
Today, the fastest lifts can travel more than seventy kilometres an hour.
Our fridge keeps food fresh for many days.
Fruit and vegetables go in the bottom drawers.
Meat and fish go in the freezer.
Please close the door quickly so the cold air stays inside.
Before electric fridges, keeping food fresh was a big problem, especially in hot countries.
People dried meat and fish in the sun, or they kept them in salt.
Water was stored in clay pots, which kept it cool because a little water passed through the clay and dried in the air.
The first fridges for homes appeared about one hundred years ago.
Today, a fridge is in almost every kitchen, but it uses a lot of electricity, so we should not leave the door open.
Hamad and his mother are waiting at the traffic lights.
The light for the cars is green, so they must wait.
Now the cars stop and the little man turns green.
They look left and right, then they cross the road.
The first traffic light was put up in London in eighteen sixty-eight, even before there were cars.
It was used to control horses and carriages, and a policeman turned it by hand.
Electric traffic lights came about fifty years later.
Today, many traffic lights are smart.
They use cameras and sensors to count the cars and change the colors at the best time.
Some cities give ambulances a green light so they can reach hospitals faster.
On Saturday, Sara helped her father with the washing.
They put the white clothes in first.
Sara added the soap and pressed the start button.
After an hour, they hung the clean clothes outside to dry.
In the past, washing clothes was one of the hardest jobs in the house.
People carried the clothes to a river or a well and washed them by hand.
It could take a whole day.
The first electric washing machines appeared about one hundred years ago, and they changed life for many families.
Today's machines can choose the right amount of water and soap by themselves.
To save water and electricity, it is best to wait until the machine is full before you use it.
At the port, giant cranes are moving containers from a huge ship.
Each container is as big as a room.
The crane driver sits high in a small cabin.
He moves the containers carefully onto the trucks.
Almost everything we buy, from toys to bananas, travels across the sea in metal containers.
Jeddah Islamic Port is one of the busiest ports in the region.
Huge ships arrive there every day carrying thousands of containers.
Giant cranes lift them off the ships, one by one.
A good crane driver can move about thirty containers in an hour.
Computers keep track of every container so that nothing gets lost.
In the car factory, robots work next to people.
The robot arms lift heavy parts and paint the cars.
People check the robots and fix them when they stop.
Together, they make hundreds of cars every day.
Robots are machines that can do jobs by themselves after people program them.
In factories, they do work that is boring, heavy or dangerous for humans.
Some hospitals use robots to help doctors with very careful operations.
In some cities, small robots deliver food and parcels along the pavement.
Robots are good at repeating the same task many times, but they still need people to design them, program them and decide what is right.
In the middle of the old village there was a deep well.
Every morning the women and girls came with their buckets.
They pulled up the water with a long rope.
It was also a place to meet and talk.
Once upon a time, a village in the desert had only one well.
One hot summer, the water became lower and lower.
The people were worried.
A young girl named Salma noticed that the birds always flew towards the same hill in the evening.
She followed them with her father and found a small spring of fresh water behind the rocks.
The villagers dug a new well there, and they named it Salma's Well in her honour.
Long ago, caravans of camels crossed the Arabian desert.
The traders carried spices, cloth and incense from the south to the north.
They travelled at night when it was cooler.
The camels could walk for days without water.
For more than a thousand years, the incense road ran through Arabia.
Caravans with hundreds of camels carried frankincense from Oman and Yemen to the cities of the north.
Towns grew up along the road where the travellers stopped for water and food.
One of these towns was Al-Ula, where you can still see tombs carved into the rock.
The caravans brought not only goods but also news, stories and new ideas from far away.
Uncle Mubarak has a beautiful falcon called Shaheen.
He trains it every morning in the desert.
Shaheen sits on his glove and watches everything with its sharp eyes.
When Uncle Mubarak whistles, the falcon flies back to him.
Falconry is one of the oldest traditions in Arabia.
In the past, Bedouins trained falcons to hunt birds and rabbits, which gave them food in the desert.
A falconer and his bird build a strong friendship based on trust.
The falcon wears a small leather hood over its eyes to keep it calm.
Today, falconry is a popular sport, and some falcons are even given their own passports to travel to competitions in other countries.
The old shepherd sat by the fire with his grandson.
He pointed at the sky and said, look, that is the North Star.
If you walk towards it, you are going north.
The boy looked up and tried to remember.
Once, a young traveller got lost in the desert at night.
He had no map and his phone had no battery.
He remembered his grandmother's advice: when you are lost, be calm and look up.
He found the North Star and remembered that his village was to the north.
He walked slowly through the night, always keeping the star in front of him.
At sunrise, he saw the palm trees of his village.
From that day, he always taught children the names of the stars.
After a long day in the desert, the travellers saw green palm trees in the distance.
It was an oasis!
They hurried there and drank cool water from the spring.
Then they rested in the shade until the evening.
Al-Ahsa in the east of Saudi Arabia is one of the largest oases in the world.
It has more than two and a half million palm trees, which grow because there is water deep under the ground.
For thousands of years, farmers there have grown dates, rice and vegetables.
In the past, water from natural springs flowed through small channels to every farm.
Today, Al-Ahsa is a World Heritage Site, and visitors come from many countries to see it.
A young shepherd looked after his family's sheep near the mountains.
Every night, he counted them carefully.
One evening, one little sheep was missing.
He took his torch and went to look for it.
A clever shepherd had a problem.
Every night, a hungry wolf came close to his sheep.
He did not want to hurt the wolf, but he had to protect his animals.
So he collected thorny branches and built a strong fence around the sheep.
He also lit a small fire, because wolves are afraid of fire.
When the wolf came, it saw the fire and could not get through the thorns.
After a few nights, it gave up and went away to look for food in the mountains.
The Al-Harbi family has just arrived at the airport.
They have checked in their bags, and now they are waiting at gate seven.
Their flight to Istanbul has been delayed by forty minutes.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is one of the busiest airports in the region.
Every day, thousands of passengers pass through its terminals.
Before a flight, passengers must check in, either online or at the desk, and drop off their large bags.
Then they go through passport control and security, where their hand luggage is checked by machines.
After that, they can relax in the waiting area until their gate opens.
Experienced travellers say the best advice is simple: always arrive early, and keep your passport in a safe place.
Huda and her grandmother are on the train from Riyadh to Al-Qassim.
They have been travelling for an hour.
Outside the window, the desert looks golden in the afternoon sun.
The North-South railway is one of the longest railways in the Middle East.
It crosses huge areas of desert, connecting Riyadh with cities in the north of the country.
Building it was a great challenge because sand dunes move with the wind and can cover the tracks.
Engineers built special fences and planted bushes to stop the sand.
Today, passengers can relax in comfortable seats, eat a meal and watch the changing landscape.
Many people say that travelling by train is calmer than driving on long desert roads.
Sami and his father were lost in Istanbul.
They had walked for an hour, but they couldn't find their hotel.
A kind shop owner showed them the way on a map.
The hotel was just around the corner.
Getting lost in a new city can be frightening, but it can also be an adventure.
Before you go out, it is a good idea to write the name and address of your hotel on a card.
If your phone stops working, you can show the card to a taxi driver.
Try to remember big landmarks, such as a tall tower or a mosque.
If you need help, ask a shop owner or a police officer rather than a stranger in the street.
Most people are happy to help a polite visitor.
Before the hike, the scout leader gave everyone a map.
He showed them how to use the key to understand the symbols.
Blue lines are rivers, and brown lines show the mountains.
People have been making maps for thousands of years.
One of the most famous mapmakers in history was Al-Idrisi, who lived about nine hundred years ago.
He travelled widely and collected information from sailors and traders.
Then he made a world map that was the most accurate of its time.
It was so good that people used it for three hundred years.
Today, we use maps on our phones, but they still depend on the same ideas: scale, symbols and direction.
Dear Grandma, we have been in Abha for three days.
The weather is cool, and we have walked in the green mountains every day.
I have bought you a small present.
I miss you.
Love, Reem.
Before phones and email, letters were the main way to send news to family far away.
A letter could take weeks to arrive, so people wrote long, careful messages.
Many families still keep old letters in boxes, and reading them is like opening a window to the past.
Today, writing a letter by hand has become rare, which makes it even more special.
A handwritten card shows that you have taken time to think about someone.
Why not write one this week to a person you love?
After two weeks in Malaysia, the Al-Otaibi family has come home.
The children are tired but happy.
They have brought souvenirs for their cousins.
Tonight, everyone is coming to see the photos.
Coming home after a long journey is a special feeling.
Your own bed feels softer, and the food tastes better than anywhere else.
Many travellers say that a trip helps them see their home with new eyes.
They notice things they had never noticed before, like the friendly neighbours or the beautiful sunset over the city.
Unpacking can be boring, but it is also a chance to remember every moment of the journey.
Some families make a photo book together so they can enjoy the memories for years.
Nasser has been tired at school this week.
He has been playing games on his tablet until midnight.
His teacher has advised him to switch off all screens one hour before bedtime.
Scientists have discovered that sleep is not just rest.
While we sleep, the brain is very busy.
It sorts the information we learned during the day and stores the important parts as memories.
That is why sleeping well before a test is better than studying all night.
Children of nine or ten need about ten hours of sleep.
Without enough sleep, it is harder to concentrate, and people often feel grumpy.
A regular bedtime, a dark room and no screens can all help you sleep better.
Babies are born with about three hundred bones.
As they grow, some of the bones join together.
That is why adults have fewer bones than babies.
Your bones and muscles work together like a team.
Bones give your body its shape and protect important parts, like your brain and heart.
Muscles are attached to bones, and when a muscle pulls, the bone moves.
You have more than six hundred muscles in your body.
Some of them, like the heart, work all the time without you thinking about it.
To keep your bones and muscles healthy, you need calcium, protein and plenty of exercise.
Close your eyes and listen.
What can you hear?
Maybe a car outside, or the wind.
When we can't see, our other senses work harder.
We usually talk about five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.
Each sense sends messages to the brain through nerves.
The brain puts all the messages together so we understand the world around us.
Some animals have senses much stronger than ours.
Eagles can see a rabbit from more than two kilometres away, and sharks can smell a drop of blood in a huge amount of water.
Scientists now say that humans have more than five senses, including the sense of balance.
Our bodies need fuel, just like cars.
Food gives us energy to run, think and grow.
A healthy plate has vegetables, protein, grains and some fruit.
Not all foods give us energy in the same way.
Sugary snacks give a quick burst of energy, but it doesn't last long, and soon you feel tired again.
Foods like oats, brown bread and beans release their energy slowly, so you can concentrate for longer.
Drinking enough water is also important, because even a little thirst can make it harder to think.
Nutritionists suggest that half of our plate should be vegetables and fruit.
They also remind us that breakfast is an important meal for students.
Germs are tiny living things.
They are too small to see without a microscope.
Some germs make us sick, so we should wash our hands before eating and after using the toilet.
Not all germs are bad.
In fact, millions of helpful bacteria live in our stomachs and help us digest food.
However, some germs cause illnesses like colds and flu.
They can spread through coughs, sneezes and dirty hands.
Washing your hands with soap is one of the simplest ways to stay healthy.
Soap breaks down the outside layer of many germs and washes them away.
Doctors say that clean hands have saved more lives than many medicines.
During break time, Omar fell and hurt his knee.
His friend Ali stayed calm and called the teacher.
The school nurse cleaned the cut and put a plaster on it.
Omar was back in class after ten minutes.
First aid is the help you give someone before a doctor or an ambulance arrives.
You don't need to be an adult to learn basic first aid.
Many schools now teach children what to do in an emergency.
The most important rule is to stay safe yourself and call for help.
For a small cut, wash it with clean water and cover it.
For a burn, cool it under running water for at least ten minutes.
Knowing these simple steps can make a big difference.
Lulu was looking at the birds in the garden.
If I were a bird, she said, I would fly to my grandmother's house every day.
It would only take ten minutes!
Many birds make incredible journeys every year.
If you were an Arctic tern, you would fly from the top of the world to the bottom and back again, about seventy thousand kilometres a year.
Some birds that pass through Saudi Arabia travel between Europe and Africa.
They stop at our lakes and coasts to rest and eat.
Scientists still do not fully understand how birds find their way, but they think birds use the sun, the stars and even the Earth's magnetic field.
When Fatima grows up, she wants to be a vet.
She loves animals and wants to help them when they are sick.
She already volunteers at an animal shelter on Saturdays.
When our grandparents were young, there were fewer kinds of jobs.
Today, there are jobs that did not exist twenty years ago, such as app designer or drone pilot.
By the time you grow up, there may be jobs that nobody has imagined yet.
That is why many teachers say the most important skills are learning how to learn, working with others and solving problems.
Whatever you choose, it helps to follow what you love and to keep practising.
In some countries, it has not rained for months.
The ground is dry and cracked.
Farmers cannot grow their crops, and animals have to walk far to find water.
If it never rained, life on land would be almost impossible.
Rain fills rivers, lakes and the water deep under the ground.
In dry countries like ours, every drop is precious.
Long ago, people built underground channels called aflaj to carry water to their farms without losing it to the sun.
Today, some cities collect rainwater from roofs and store it in tanks.
Scientists are also testing ways to make clouds produce more rain.
But the easiest thing everyone can do is not to waste water.
Before the trip, Mum wrote a checklist.
Passports, tickets, charger, medicine and sunscreen.
Everyone checked their own bag.
Only then did they lock the house and leave.
A good trip starts long before you leave home.
First, check that everyone's passport is valid for at least six months.
Some countries also ask for a visa, which can take weeks to arrive.
Find out about the weather so you can pack the right clothes.
If you are going somewhere hot, pack light clothes, a hat and plenty of sunscreen.
It is also wise to make copies of important documents in case they get lost.
Finally, learn a few words of the local language.
People really appreciate it.
It was seven fifteen.
Unless Hamad hurried, he would miss the school bus.
He grabbed his bag and his sandwich and ran outside.
The bus was just arriving.
Some people are always on time, and others are always rushing.
Being on time is a skill that you can learn.
Start by getting ready the night before: pack your bag and choose your clothes.
Set your alarm a few minutes earlier than you need.
Unless you plan ahead, small things like a lost shoe can make you late.
Being on time shows respect for other people's time.
In many jobs, it is one of the most valued habits.
Yousef saw a younger boy alone in the playground.
He was crying because the other children wouldn't play with him.
Yousef asked him to join his team.
The boy smiled for the first time that day.
Our class played a game called What Would You Do.
The teacher read a situation, and we discussed the best choice.
In one situation, you see a classmate copying during a test.
Some students said they would tell the teacher immediately.
Others said they would talk to the classmate first.
There was no single right answer, but everyone agreed that honesty matters.
The teacher said that thinking about these situations now helps us make better decisions later.
Dad couldn't find the car key anywhere.
He had looked in his pockets and on the table.
Then Lina noticed the cat playing with something shiny under the sofa.
It was the missing key!
Detectives solve mysteries by collecting clues and thinking carefully.
They don't guess; they look for facts.
A good detective notices small details, like a muddy footprint or a cup that is still warm.
They ask questions and listen carefully to the answers.
Then they put all the clues together, like pieces of a puzzle.
Sometimes the answer is surprising.
Famous fictional detectives, such as Sherlock Holmes, have taught readers that careful observation is the key to the truth.
After the rain, Saud found strange footprints in the garden.
They were small and had three toes.
He followed them to the bushes, where he found a hedgehog eating insects.
Footprints can tell us a surprising amount of information.
Police experts can work out a person's height from the length of their footprint.
The depth of the print can show if the person was carrying something heavy.
Animal trackers in the desert can read footprints like a book.
They can tell which animal passed, how fast it was moving and even how long ago it was there.
In the past, Bedouin trackers were so skilled that they were often asked to help find lost camels.
The museum guard opened the room in the morning.
The window was closed, and the door had been locked all night.
But the golden cup had disappeared!
The police were called immediately.
The case of the golden cup confused everyone.
The door was locked, the window was shut, and there were no footprints.
Detective Noura looked around the room slowly.
She noticed a small hole in the ceiling above the table.
On the floor, there was a tiny piece of string.
She realised that the thief had lowered a hook through the hole and lifted the cup out.
The guard who worked upstairs had a hook in his bag.
The mystery of the locked room was solved.
On Tuesday, Majid found a note in his school bag.
It said: meet me at the library at break time.
There was no name on it.
At break time, he went to the library and found his best friend waiting with a birthday card.
People have been sending secret messages for thousands of years.
One simple method is to swap each letter for the next one in the alphabet, so A becomes B and B becomes C.
Another method is invisible ink.
If you write with lemon juice and let it dry, the message disappears.
When the paper is warmed carefully by an adult, the writing turns brown and appears again.
During history, some secret codes were so difficult that it took teams of experts years to break them.
While cleaning the attic, Hessa found an old map.
It showed the family farm, and there was an X under the big palm tree.
With her father's help, she dug a hole and found a metal box.
Inside were old photos and coins.
Archaeologists are scientists who study the past by digging up old objects.
Unlike treasure hunters in films, they work very slowly and carefully.
They use small brushes to clean the sand from each object and record exactly where it was found.
In Saudi Arabia, archaeologists have found ancient tools, writing and even footprints that are thousands of years old.
Each discovery is like a piece of a giant puzzle that helps us understand how people lived long ago.
Everyone gathered in the hall.
Detective Faris explained how he had solved the mystery.
The missing laptop had been taken by mistake.
It was in the teacher's car all the time!
At the end of every good mystery story, the detective explains the solution.
This is often the most exciting part, because readers can check whether they guessed correctly.
A well-written mystery gives readers all the clues they need, but hides them cleverly.
Writers call misleading clues red herrings, because they send the reader in the wrong direction.
If you enjoy mysteries, try writing your own.
Start with the solution, then plan the clues backwards.
The Amazon rainforest is the largest rainforest in the world.
Millions of different animals and plants live there.
Some scientists call it the lungs of the planet.
People often think that Saudi Arabia has no forests, but that is not true.
In the southwest, in the mountains of Asir and Al-Baha, there are forests of juniper trees.
Some of these trees are hundreds of years old.
The cooler weather and the rain in summer help them grow.
Recently, the country started a huge project to plant ten billion trees.
The trees will help stop the desert from spreading and give shade and homes to wildlife.
It begins in the mountains and ends in the Mediterranean Sea.
For thousands of years, it has given water to farmers along its banks.
Although Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers, it has thousands of wadis.
Most of the year, a wadi is a dry valley where you can walk or camp.
But after heavy rain, water rushes down from the mountains and the wadi can become a fast river in minutes.
These floods are dangerous, and every year people are warned not to drive through flooded wadis.
At the same time, the water brings life.
It fills underground wells and makes the desert bloom with flowers.
In some parts of the world, deserts are growing every year.
When people cut down trees and animals eat all the grass, the soil becomes loose.
Then the wind blows it away.
In Africa, countries are working together on a project called the Great Green Wall.
The plan is to plant a wide belt of trees and bushes across the continent, from west to east, at the edge of the Sahara desert.
The plants hold the soil, keep water in the ground and give farmers land to grow food again.
In some villages, the project has already brought back crops and jobs.
It shows that people can slow down the desert when they work together.
The Arabian leopard is one of the rarest animals in the world.
Fewer than two hundred live in the wild.
Scientists in Saudi Arabia are breeding leopards to help them survive.
By the early nineteen seventies, the Arabian oryx had disappeared from the wild.
People had hunted it too much.
Fortunately, a few oryx were living in zoos and private collections.
Scientists brought them together and carefully raised more young.
Years later, they released them into protected reserves in Saudi Arabia, Oman and other countries.
Today, there are more than a thousand oryx in the wild.
It is one of the greatest success stories in protecting animals, and it shows that it is never too late to help.
On the roof of our school, there are many solar panels.
They change sunlight into electricity.
On sunny days, they make enough power for all the classrooms.
For a long time, most electricity has been made by burning oil, gas or coal.
This creates pollution and adds gases that warm the planet.
Renewable energy comes from sources that do not run out, like the sun and the wind.
Saudi Arabia has some of the sunniest land in the world, which makes it perfect for solar power.
Huge solar farms are being built in the desert.
The country plans to make half of its electricity from renewable sources in the coming years.
Last month, Ahmed's class started a recycling project.
They put three bins in every classroom: one for paper, one for plastic and one for cans.
In four weeks, they collected two hundred kilograms of waste.
When we hear about big problems like pollution, it is easy to feel that one person cannot change anything.
But small actions, repeated by millions of people, make a huge difference.
If every family in a city used one less plastic bag a day, millions of bags would be saved every year.
Children can be powerful too.
They can remind their families to save water, share ideas at school and start projects in their neighbourhood.
Protecting our planet is not one big action.
It is many small choices every day.
